title: Silver roofs
hook: if not for people all becoming one in disbelief, the deniers would have had silver roofs, and it's all the enjoyment of this life (43:33–35)

segments.voice: Yesterday, hiba, daughters and sons, and your line was each gift is his. Did a girl in your life hear that she's a gift? Today, a new surah, Az-Zukhruf, the Ornaments. Day five hundred seventy.

'Umar walks into a small room in Medina and finds the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lying on a rough mat of palm fiber, with nothing between it and his skin. When he sits up, the weave has left lines pressed into his side. A leather pillow stuffed with fiber. A little barley in the corner. 'Umar looks around and starts to cry. He's thinking of the kings of Persia and Rome, in their palaces, and here is the Messenger of Allah on a mat. The Prophet asks him why he's crying. His answer, in Bukhari, is close to today's verses.

Surah Az-Zukhruf, verses thirty-three to thirty-five. The surah is pushing back on a claim it quotes a few verses earlier: if this message were true, wouldn't it have come to some great man of the two cities, someone rich? So the Qur'an answers with an image. If it weren't that all people would become one community of deniers, chasing it, Allah would have given those who deny the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and silver stairways to climb, and doors, and couches to lean on, and zukhruf, gold ornament. Then the verdict: all of that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world, and the hereafter with your Lord is for the mindful. Commentators draw out the point: in this picture, silver roofs are so slight a thing they could be handed to people who reject Him, except that everyone would then chase the silver. In the verse, wealth isn't a sign of being favored, and it isn't the scale anyone is weighed on. Zukhruf, the surah's name, means gold, and the ornament laid over a surface. Beautiful, and on the outside. Back to 'Umar in the little room. The Prophet answered him: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the hereafter? Not a rule against owning things; the companions included merchants and the wealthy. A rule about where the weight goes. And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says it even more sharply: if this world were worth a mosquito's wing to Allah, He wouldn't give a denier a sip of water from it.
screen: `THEY HAVE THIS WORLD; WE, THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice an ornament you want. Sit, and let something come to mind that you've wanted lately: a phone, a kitchen, a car, a look, a kind of house. Don't judge the wanting. Just see it clearly. Now picture it a few years from now: scratched, out of date, replaced. Notice which part of you still wants it after that. Then let it rest, lightly, like gold leaf. The bell holds the time.
Silver roofs. Az-Zukhruf's picture: silver roofs and gold ornament, so cheap to Allah He'd give them to deniers, all only the enjoyment of this life. Today's word.
Your line: ornaments pass. Today, when you catch yourself wanting something shiny, ask: will this still matter when the gilding wears off? Day five hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Muslim teaching on zuhd, detachment from worldly things, often cites Az-Zukhruf 33–35 and the Prophet's simple room; many Muslims understand wealth as a trust to be used well, not a sign of God's favor.

fork.setup: you're 'Umar, crying at the Prophet's mat while kings live in palaces. what does the Prophet say?
options: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we the hereafter?
don't cry; it's only a mat.
fork.reveal: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the hereafter? the weight goes on what lasts.

original.note: Arabic: gold ornament, gilding, the name of surah forty-three.

trapdoor: what you thought: money is bad.
what it means: silver roofs and gold ornament are only this life's enjoyment, too cheap to be the measure of anyone.
what a scholar hears: 43:31–35 answers the demand for a rich prophet; zukhruf is gilding; Bukhari 4913 has 'Umar and the mat, and Tirmidhi 2320 the mosquito's wing.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4913; Sahih Muslim 1479 ('Umar and the mat)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 4913, Muslim 1479, Tirmidhi 2320) cited from memory; confirm.
The hook's details (leather pillow stuffed with fiber, barley) follow the 'Umar report; confirm.
'Kings of Persia and Rome' is from the report itself and is not used to rank anyone.

Editor review: narrator no longer states 'cheap in Allah's eyes' as fact (now the commentators' reading); 'zukhruf means gold leaf, thin' was a preacher's gloss, now 'gold, ornament'; full first naming of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
